articles.title: England rugby: Shaun Edwards' Red Roses move inspired by mother - Marlie Packer
articles.summary: England back row Marlie Packer says defence coach Shaun Edwards' surprise move into the Red Roses set-up was partly inspired by his late mother Phyllis.
articles.body:
England back row Marlie Packer says defence coach Shaun Edwards' surprise move into the Red Roses set-up was partly inspired by his late mother Phyllis.

Edwards has joined the world champions for the remainder of their autumn campaign after the end of a six-and-a half-year stint with France.

"He told us a little story, telling us why he wanted to be here," said Packer.

"He was saying about his mum not ever being able to have the opportunity to play, and that she would have loved to have done so.

"It was really cool to hear that she thought we were amazing."

Phyllis Edwards worked as a hairdresser in the family's hometown of Wigan, but was a trusted advisor throughout her son's career. She also cared for Edwards' father Jackie after his own career with league side Warrington was ended by a spinal injury at the age of 24.

"Back in the mid-1990s she was the first person to tell me to study rugby union as well as rugby league, because I always wanted to be a coach and I always took notes of what coaches said," said Edwards at the time.

"When rugby union went professional in 1995, I was at the top of the league game, captain of Wigan who were world champions, but she always told me to learn about rugby union."

Edwards' study paid off. After lifting domestic and European titles during his time coaching club side Wasps, he has won a total of seven Six Nations crowns across stints with Wales and France.

"He's got more Six Nations than quite a few of the girls, to be fair to him!" added Packer, who has been part of 10 Grand Slam-winning sides herself since making her England debut in 2008.

"To have that calibre of coach to want to come and work with the Red Roses, just showcases where the women's game is going and what this Red Roses team has done and are doing.

"He's straight talking. He doesn't say too much, but when he does say something, you hear it."

England's winning run was halted on 39 successive Tests last weekend, when Canada held them to a 26-26 draw at Sandy Park.

England take on New Zealand, the Red Roses' closest challengers at the top of the world rankings, at Allianz Stadium on Saturday, before crossing the Atlantic next month for matches against Canada in Ottawa and Toronto, and a Test against the United States.

"We're not happy with the draw, but we didn't lose a match," said Packer.

"It was a really great game of rugby. If you're a neutral that's the kind of rugby that you want to come and watch - you don't know who's going to win, end-to-end scoring, and such a physical, physical game.

"We know we have to build from last week. We're in a Test series against Canada; that's our first game, now we've got two away legs. We know what we have got to put right."

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

The WXV Global Series - the new event designed to increase the number and competitiveness of Test matches in the autumn for the world's best women - has delivered several superb games.

In addition to England's draw against Canada, last weekend featured France recovering from 19 points down to beat Australia 29-26 and the United States overhauling a 17-point deficit to see off Ireland 40-36 in Dublin.

Australia also came hard at England on the opening weekend of matches, leading 10-5 at half-time in Salford before succumbing to a 48-15 defeat.

"The Red Roses are always pushing that bar higher, then it's for the other teams to raise their game, that's exactly what's happening and that's what we want as players," Packer added.

"The more the game goes professional, the more the unions put money into their women's sides, we're going to see better contests of rugby.

"We're going to see that the Red Roses have it won in the first half. There will have to be 80-minute performances.

"We don't want to turn up and have to have targets within games because we know we're going to win. We want to be in a rugby contest."

The Black Ferns were the last team to beat England, upsetting them in the Women's Rugby World Cup final at Eden Park in November 2022.

They come into Saturday's contest under the leadership of Whitney Hansen, who has won all seven Tests since taking over as head coach in December, including a 36-14 victory over Canada in April in Kansas.

The match against England takes place a day before the one-year anniversary of the Red Roses' Rugby World Cup final triumph in front of a capacity 81,855 Twickenham crowd.

Packer says the focus for the team is forward however.

"That's history now to us," she said. "It's a massive thing - we can celebrate that World Cup, but actually this squad is very different from that World Cup squad.

"We've become Grand Slam champions since then and we're building to perform really well at WXV.

A Rugby Football Union report says hosting the World Cup has been the catalyst for a jump in playing numbers in the girls' and women's game.

The number of girls aged six to 12 playing rugby in clubs grew from 18,000 to 26,800 over the course of four years of investment from government totalling £14.6m.

"Today, more women and girls are playing, coaching and officiating rugby than ever before," said Alex Teasdale, the RFU's executive director of the women's game.

"Across England, we have seen communities come together to break down barriers, challenge perceptions and open the door to a new generation of participants."

articles.title: Man of Steel 2026: Brad O'Neill, Adam Keighran and Lachie Miller named on three-player shortlist
articles.summary: The winner of the Man of Steel award will be announced on Tuesday September 29; Jake Connor is the reigning Man of Steel but is not on the shortlist; The play-offs are under way, live on Sky Sports, and continue through until the Grand Final from Old Trafford on October 3
articles.body:
A panel made up of five former Man of Steel winners; Ellery Hanley, Sam Tomkins, James Roby, Joe Lydon and Paul Sculthorpe, narrowed down the 12-player list into a final three.

The panel met three times across the season to look at rounds 1-9, 10-18, and 19-27 and came up with a top five for each third.

Players who had made it into a top five across the season were: O'Neill, Keighran, Miller, Jake Connor, Umyla Hanley, Jez Litten, Tyrone May, Brodie Croft, Daryl Clark, Ash Handley, Bevan French, and Jai Field.

Reigning Man of Steel Connor has not made the final shortlist despite a brilliant season for Leeds Rhinos in which he came up with 43 assists, nearly double the amount of any other playmaker in the competition.

Hanley was also included in the panel's top five on two occasions, the only player to achieve such a feat alongside O'Neill and Miller, but is not in the top three.

Keighran was included in the top five from the panel for the final third of the season.

Combative hooker O'Neill has already claimed the Rugby League Writers and Broadcasters Association (RLWBA) Player of the Year award having helped Wigan to the League Leaders' Shield, the Challenge Cup and within 80 minutes of the Grand Final.

With his tough-tackling, pinpoint passing and impressive durability, the 24-year-old has developed into an integral part of Matt Peet's Treble-chasing side.

Australian full-back Miller has been in the Man of Steel conversation since the opening weeks of the season, when he came out on top in the panel's first vote after the opening nine rounds.

No player has made more than the electric Leeds full-back's 166 tackle busts this term and his brilliant running game has lit up plenty of contests for Rhinos, who were long-time league leaders.

Keighran finished the regular campaign with 16 tries and 107 goals, but he has also earned praise for his hard-hitting defence and classy partnership with free-scoring winger Zach Eckersley.

Semi-Final 2 - Saturday September 26: Wigan Warriors v Wakefield Trinity, 5.30pm KO on Sky Sports

articles.title: Australia vs South Africa: Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus makes 13 changes to starting side for Perth Test after series win over All Blacks
articles.summary: South Africa have made 13 changes to the side that won the three-match series against the All Blacks to take on Australia in Perth; Watch Australia take on South Africa in a one-off Test on Sunday September 27, with kick-off at 10.45am, live on Sky Sports+
articles.body:
Only lock Eben Etzebeth and winger Ethan Hooker retained their starting roles from the team that beat the All Blacks 43-28 in Baltimore to seal a 3-1 win in the inaugural Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.

Etzebeth will extend his record as the most capped Springbok of all time to 147 Test matches.

Props Jan-Hendrik Wessels and Zachary Porthen will join forces with hooker Johan Grobbelaar in a new-look front row, while two-time World Cup-winning fly-half Handre Pollard returns from a calf injury to form a new halves pairing with fit-again scrum-half Herschel Jantjies.

Centre Andre Esterhuizen has been named skipper, making him South Africa's 68th captain.

Lock Franco Mostert will play his first Test since facing Wales last November.

Despite the mass changes, only three players named in the starting lineup have fewer than 10 Test caps - winger Edwill van der Merwe, lock Paul de Villiers and prop Porthen.

"Australia poses a completely different threat to New Zealand in the way they play, so we believe these combinations would be best suited for the challenge that we will face against them," South Africa coach Rassie Erasmus said.

"This is going to be a big challenge against a team that has been playing good rugby, and who have won four of their last five matches, with their other result being a draw against the Pumas in Argentina."

Erasmus had no second thoughts about allowing veteran duo Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende to return home so they could spend time with family.

"They had a heavy workload in the last few months, and they deserve a break," Erasmus said.

Australia head coach Les Kiss is expected to name his side on Friday with reports centre Joseph Suaalii is set to be handed a start on the wing.

articles.title: WXV: Wales' Seren Lockwood out of USA Test with Carys Cox set for return
articles.summary: Scrum-half Seren Lockwood is out of Wales' second WXV Test, against USA, after failing a head injury assessment.
articles.body:
Scrum-half Seren Lockwood has been ruled out of Wales' second WXV Global Series fixture, against USA in Cardiff on Saturday, after failing a head injury assessment.

Lockwood was taken off during the first half of Wales' eight-try victory over South Africa and is now going through World Rugby's return to play protocols.

It is a blow for Wales with Lockwood and Keira Bevan proving a promising half-back partnership in a new-look backline.

Her absence paves the way for Lleucu George to return at 10, with Bevan reverting to her usual position of nine at Cardiff Arms Park.

"It's always sad to see an individual coming off, but the HIA is great to have on board, we're looking after her," said Wales head coach Sean Lynn.

"She's not going to be available this weekend, but I'm super excited to see the half-back combination that we've got this week."

Wales deliver performance of serious promise

Inspired Wales seal stunning win over South Africa

Carys Cox's return to fitness after summer knee surgery gives Lynn another option in the backline, with Cox able to play centre and on the wing.

"Carys has been superb in rehab, she feels fitter, faster and stronger," said Lynn.

"She always brings a smile, she's always confident and I love her athleticism. She will always beat that first defender and the way we are playing now, she's going to get some ball in hand."

Saturday's game at Cardiff Arms Park comes too soon for fellow back Nel Metcalfe, who will not be ready until next month's two-Test tour of Japan.

"Nel is progressing really well with her rehab, we saw her today in some rugby elements, so fingers crossed we will be seeing her in Japan," Lynn added.

articles.title: United Rugby Championship: Ulster's James Hume ruled out of Edinburgh opener
articles.summary: Ulster centre James Hume is ruled out of Ulster's United Rugby Championship season opener against Edinburgh with a hamstring injury.
articles.body:
Ulster head coach Richie Murphy says he expects centre James Hume to be missing for "a number of weeks" after the centre was ruled out of the province's season opener.

Hume suffered a hamstring injury in training this week before Friday's United Rugby Championship opener against Edinburgh at Affidea Stadium (19:45 BST).

His absence will come as a major blow to Murphy, who is already missing midfield options Jude Postlethwaite and Stewart Moore through injury.

Centre David Hawkshaw arrived during the summer.

"James picked up a muscle injury during the week which was an awful pity because he'd put in a huge amount of work and was probably looking the fittest he'd looked in a number of years," Murphy told BBC Sport NI.

"It's disappointing for James and for us as a team.

"But one man goes down, the next man stands up so it'll be an opportunity for someone else."

The Ulster coach added that the 28-year-old could return to action before the conclusion of the series of matches leading up to the break for Ireland's November internationals.

"He'll be out for a number of weeks. It's hard to say at the moment, it's very early in that injury. There's a possibility he'll be back before the end of the block but we're not sure at the moment."

A squad update issued by Ulster Rugby on Wednesday indicated that three other players - Juarno Augustus and summer signings Matthew Devine and Keynan Knox - had participated in team training after overcoming their respective injuries.

articles.title: Henry Pollock: Northampton chief expects more players to work with promoters like Eddie Hearn as he lifts lid on negotiations
articles.summary: Henry Pollock put pen to paper on a new multi-year deal with boyhood club Northampton Saints on Tuesday; he had signed with Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom Talent Agency earlier this year
articles.body:
On Tuesday, Pollock put pen to paper on a multi-year extension with his boyhood club , with the England international agreeing a deal worth £400,000 per year.

At just 21, Pollock already has 13 England caps and made five appearances for the British & Irish Lions during last year's tour of Australia.

Pollock's profile continues to grow, with the flanker becoming the first rugby union player to join Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency at the start of the year. Dowson revealed that the boxing promoter "drove as hard a bargain as he possibly could" during negotiations.

Reflecting on Pollock's decision to join Hearn's agency, Dowson said: "I think we'll see more of it.

"I think headlines and social media engagement, and all that, is positive for the game. Fundamentally, I talked to the coaches about this. We want more people watching the game, more people talking about the game and, ideally, most importantly, more people playing the game at loads of different age groups.

"If Henry Pollock and Matchroom are getting some traction with the public, I think we should encourage that, but also take into account that we've got to continue to deliver that in the right way, and I think we have them."

Hearn told The Telegraph that he believes the 21-year-old is worth more than seven figures, predicting Pollock's value will "skyrocket" over the coming years while also arguing that the value of rugby will rise.

Dowson also lifted the lid on the boxing promoter's role in the negotiations, lauding him for helping him grow Pollock's profile, adding that part of the negotiations were handled by a "traditional rugby agent".

"Eddie's been excellent. He's raised the profile of the game," Dowson said.

"He's raised the profile of Henry and he's done what an agent's supposed to do. He's driven as hard a bargain as he possibly could.

"I've got a lot of respect for Eddie and how he goes about his work and some of the stuff he said in the media was really pertinent.

"I think there's elements of the contract which weren't done by Eddie, which were done by his traditional rugby agent.

"There are things from a marketing point of view and the extracurricular stuff that Eddie really looks after Pollock with, which we'll see more of.

"He wasn't necessarily doing every single negotiation from a rugby point of view."

Pollock has explained in the past that he had an open mind to the next steps of his career, but on Tuesday said he was "massively happy to re-sign with Saints".

Some fans had questioned why the negotiations had taken so long to complete, with the flanker's loyalty coming under scrutiny, but Dowson said the process was made easier by Pollock's desire to stay.

"It's still his job, it's still his career. He needs to make sure he's getting the right deal for his aspirations and all those other elements that come with it," Dowson said. "I don't just mean from a financial point of view; I mean from a full, holistic perspective."

"Would there be loyalty in sport if he wasn't offered a contract? Would that be us not being loyal? I think we've got to be careful around that.

"He's playing really well. He's got lots of people talking about rugby. That's great. We wanted to keep him and he wanted to stay. That's a great position for us to start negotiations from, and that's the great thing about sport.

"People can have an opinion around it, but I don't think it was overly dragged out, to be honest, and I don't think it was ever done... there was no animosity in any way from my perspective."

articles.title: United Rugby Championship: Guide to Welsh clubs' chances in the 2026-27 season
articles.summary: BBC Sport Wales looks at the prospects for Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship season.
articles.body:
Perhaps it is down to the hope and excitement of pre-season but all four Welsh clubs go into the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship (URC) with dreams of making the play-offs.

Last season Cardiff were the only side from Wales to make the top eight while Scarlets and Ospreys were the sole Welsh representatives in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

Those three, and Dragons, have shown they can mix it with the best in the league on their day and all will feel the top eight is not out of reach if they have some luck with injury.

They will attempt to set the tone for the season in the first block of the URC, with Saturday's meeting between Scarlets and Cardiff in Llanelli the first of five derbies before the break for the November internationals.

BBC Sport Wales assess the chances of all four Welsh teams for the coming season.

Wales beat the Boks and the rest of the URC preview

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

Cardiff - Aiming to repeat play-off qualification

Key man: Teddy Williams - Cardiff will hope the Wales lock, their player of the year in 2024-25, can stay fit having been limited to three appearances in the past season after a dislocated right foot last October.

Prospects: The Blue and Blacks aim to celebrate their 150th anniversary by building on a strong 2025-26 when they made the play-offs for the first time.

After a blow on the eve of the season when boss Matt Sherratt left for Wales, Corniel van Zyl guided Cardiff to sixth in the table and Champions Cup qualification.

The South African is now charged with continuing an upward trend, helped by clarity about his future after being officially appointed permanent head coach in April.

"It does feel way better to know what is coming," said the former lock, who held talks with Benetton about their top job before they appointed ex-Wales boss Wayne Pivac.

"It helps to manage and plan well, whereas if you are thrown in at the deep end then you can make decisions quickly and it's not necessarily the right thing to do."

Cardiff's success was built on their formidable Arms Park record, with Scarlets the only team to beat them in the Welsh capital.

Expectations are high and they must mix top-tier European rugby with another tilt at the top eight, with a tricky five-day turnaround from Northampton in the Champions Cup to a home URC fixture with Sharks in October.

"Look at the last three years and Cardiff has grown. That's the main focus for us, to be a better team, and better individually and collectively as a club," said Van Zyl.

"We are not the cream of the crop yet, so the mission is to get better and have consistency in our performance.

"Last year we were very good at the Arms Park and we would love to replicate that, and also get better away from home. That's the challenge."

Derbies in the first block against Scarlets in Llanelli and Ospreys at St Helen's are key to that desire.

Cardiff will want to be Wales' top team once more.

Sio hopes Cardiff move leads to World Cup hat-trick

Wales back row Faletau signs new Cardiff deal

Ospreys - A new era beckons at St Helen's

Key man: Lalaki Foketi - The nine-times Wallabies centre arrives from Super Rugby side Chiefs and has the ability to prove a real game-breaker.

Wing Marika Koroibete is the more household name but Foketi can provide something that Ospreys or very few Welsh sides possess.

Prospects: It will be a fascinating season for Ospreys on and off the field.

To improve on last season's 11th place finish, Mark Jones' side must repeat the home form and their success in derbies that saw them lift the Welsh shield.

Put simply, Ospreys have to start winning more away games if they want to launch a play-off push, and they start their season in South Africa against Sharks and Lions.

"We had seven wins and two draws last season and 10 wins would normally get you in the play-offs," said Ospreys head coach Jones.

"We know we are not a million miles away and we have been in and around the play-offs and we want to be in there competing this season."

Ospreylia: How Welsh club turned to a land down under

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Ospreys have launched a recruitment drive in Australia with three Wallabies arriving in back-row forward Liam Wright, centre Foketi and wing Koroibete.

Australian fly-half Lawson Creighton has also come in to go alongside lock Ryan Smith, who was a resounding success last season.

It is policy that has excited supporters after the loss of Wales captains Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, but one that happened with uncertainty over the club's future still lingering with the WRU getting rid of a west Wales region in 2028.

The Ospreys, aided by Swansea Council, hope to secure the long-term future and do this by moving into the new seaside St Helen's home, while Wales legend Alun Wyn Jones has joined the board.

The opening home game is against the Dragons on 24 October and the Ospreys' faithful have one final major chance to demonstrate they will back their team. A successful start to the season will help that quest.

"Having your own home is massive," said Mark Jones. "The Swansea.com Stadium and Bridgend were great, but this gives us the opportunity to bring the city and the rest of the region in."

Key man: Fletcher Anderson - The number eight from New Zealand was the Welsh signing of the season last year with his powerful bursts. Once he recovers from a groin injury , Anderson will aim to avoid suffering the dreaded second season syndrome against teams that now know what he can do.

Prospects: Scarlets players and fans will expect a noticeable improvement from last season. No Champions Cup victories and 14th place in the URC was not acceptable for a side that is the most recent Welsh team to win the league in 2017.

Nigel Davies has become the permanent director of rugby with Dwayne Peel continuing as head coach.

"We were absolutely not happy with 14th," said Davies.

"I'm not going to sit here and give any predictions of where we're going to finish, but what we're going to see is a Scarlets team with intent, wanting to play quickly, wanting to excite our crowd and be hugely competitive and abrasive."

Scarlets have lost international forwards Marnus van der Merwe, Alec Hepburn and Jake Ball.

The main new signing is one-cap All Blacks flanker Cullen Grace who does not arrive until October. Scarlets will hope he has the same impact as his fellow New Zealander Anderson.

"We've had an honest review of where we were," said Davies.

"There's been a lot of work behind the scenes, a lot of detail, and we've put a lot of new processes in place.

"We've brought in new coaches and some new players. I know they're not all available at the moment, but that will come."

With doubts over the region's long-term future as the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) prepares to cut a men's professional side by 2028, all eyes will be on the team's performances this season.

Scarlets ready to come out fighting for future

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Dragons - Coping with greater expectations

Co-captains: Ben Carter and Angus O'Brien

Key man: Ryan Woodman - The loss of number eight Aaron Wainwright to Leicester is huge but the blind-side flanker can help soften the blow. After facing Barbarians with Wales last summer, the uncapped forward can put himself in the mix for the World Cup.

Prospects: Dragons' much-improved 2025-26 that has led to them setting a lofty target of being in the mix for the play-offs.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and had the biggest points swing in the URC, claiming 28 after the previous year's embarrassing tally of nine.

After four draws, Dragons feel that they can push into the race for the top eight.

They will at least want to avoid being Wales' lowest-ranked side - something they have been in 18 of 23 seasons - and end their 21-game losing streak against closest rivals Cardiff that goes back to 2015.

Dragons made just three signings and only one of them, Tonga wing Anzelo Tu'itavuki, will feature in the first block of the season.

After plenty of summers of upheaval, influential centre Aneurin Owen sees the lack of change as a positive.

"It has meant we have been able to build on last season, we've not started from scratch," he said.

"Changes can be good but they can also be disruptive. We have banked all of the stuff from last season and been able to develop our game a lot more."

Dragons travel to Benetton but then play five fixtures in Wales before the break for the Nations Championship.

They have home URC derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys, a Challenge Cup opener against Perpignan, an away fixture against Ospreys at the revamped St Helen's and then a Newport fixture versus Zebre.

"Last year it felt we didn't get our season going until December when we got a win and confidence grew," said Owen.

"We need to kick on. There were some promising signs last season, especially in the cup, but we still finished 15th.

"The challenge we have set as a group is to get after it in the league and Europe, and it all starts with this first block. We can get some momentum and belief."

Your guide to Welsh rugby's pre-season fixtures

There are four Welsh clubs to look at ahead of the 2026-27 season but it promises to be a crucial year as to whether that remains the case from 2028 onwards.

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) are pressing on with controversial plans to cut a professional men's side.

Cardiff and Dragons are poised to be given licences, leaving Ospreys and Scarlets fighting it out to be the team in the west.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of this season.

Welsh players will once again be tasked with putting uncertainty over the future to the back of their minds, a situation that could well lead to others joining the growing contingent playing in England after the loss of Wales co-captains Morgan and Lake to Gloucester.

Key man: Ryan Woodman - The loss of number eight Aaron Wainwright to Leicester is huge but the blind-side flanker can help soften the blow. After facing Barbarians with Wales last summer, the uncapped forward can put himself in the mix for the World Cup.

Prospects: Dragons' much-improved 2025-26 has led to them setting a lofty target of being in the mix for the play-offs.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and had the biggest points swing in the URC, claiming 28 after the previous year's embarrassing tally of nine.

After four draws, Dragons feel that they can push into the race for the top eight.

They will at least want to avoid being Wales' lowest-ranked side - something they have been in 18 of 23 seasons - and end their 21-game losing streak against closest rivals Cardiff that goes back to 2015.

Dragons have made just three signings and only one of them, Tonga wing Anzelo Tu'itavuki, will feature in the first block of the season.

After plenty of summers of upheaval, influential centre Aneurin Owen sees the lack of change as a positive.

"It has meant we have been able to build on last season, we've not started from scratch," he said.

"Changes can be good but they can also be disruptive. We have banked all of the stuff from last season and been able to develop our game a lot more."

Dragons travel to Benetton but then play five fixtures in Wales before the break for the Nations Championship.

They have home URC derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys, a Challenge Cup opener against Perpignan, an away fixture against Ospreys at the revamped St Helen's and then a Newport fixture versus Zebre.

"Last year it felt we didn't get our season going until December when we got a win and confidence grew," said Owen.

"We need to kick on. There were some promising signs last season, especially in the cup, but we still finished 15th.

"The challenge we have set as a group is to get after it in the league and Europe, and it all starts with this first block. We can get some momentum and belief."

There are four Welsh clubs to look at ahead of the 2026-27 season but it promises to be a crucial year as to whether that remains the case from 2028 onwards.

The Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) are pressing on with controversial plans to cut a professional men's side.

Cardiff and Dragons are poised to be given licences, leaving Ospreys and Scarlets fighting it out to be the team in the west.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of this season.

Welsh players will once again be tasked with putting uncertainty over the future to the back of their minds, a situation that could well lead to others joining the growing contingent playing in England after the loss of Wales co-captains Morgan and Lake to Gloucester.

articles.title: Prem Rugby 2026-27 club guide: Will Northampton Saints reign again or new winners rise?
articles.summary: BBC Sport commentators and reporters analyse how the 10 Prem Rugby clubs will fare ahead of the start of the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
Blink and it seems like a Prem Rugby season has only just finished but it has already been 97 days since 2025-26 wrapped up at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

A new campaign of the English top flight stretches before us, with 18 rounds of games between now and early next June, all against the backdrop of a World Cup that is just over 12 months away.

BBC Sport commentators and pundits from across England analyse what we can expect from each club when the games get under way.

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

Bath - 'Should challenge for honours again'

Dan Albutt, BBC Radio Bristol commentator

Bath's recruitment has been low-key with only two prime additions in South African number eight Dan du Preez and Scotland prop Jamie Bhatti, so the concern for them will be the loss of big ball carriers, especially prop Thomas du Toit and back-rower Alfie Barbeary.

Replacing their impact will be tough, but Bath still have a loaded squad that will once again have Scotland fly-half Finn Russell pulling the strings.

Last season's home semi-final defeat by Exeter will still sting, but head of rugby Johann van Graan has proven to be a master of learning from bad experiences and turning them into positives.

If they can, then they should challenge for honours again, but Du Toit and Barbeary are big losses and it may make that task a lot harder.

Scotland forward Josh Bayliss may be the most underrated player in the Prem; his power and pace will be a big asset to Bath in a stacked back row.

Listen to The Scrum every Tuesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Bristol and BBC Sounds.

Bristol - 'Need better luck with injuries'

Key signing: Ethan Staddon, back-row forward

Damian Derrick, BBC Points West sports reporter

Bristol Bears enter Pat Lam's 10th season with the clearly stated ambition of getting back into the top four play-off places.

Strangely for Bears, it was their attack and lack of tries that cost them last season. A second full season back in rugby union for Wales and British and Irish Lions winger Louis Rees-Zammit, along with a stated preference for the wing over full-back, should help enormously.

The continued development and influence of Bristolian prop George Kloska, now an England international, will be key. So is keeping Argentina international lock Pedro Rubiolo fit.

The depth of their squad is still a concern - particularly in the front five and at fly-half - so they'll need better luck with injuries.

Bristol's form after the mid-season Six Nations break must also improve as it's let them down over the past two seasons.

Get that right and Lam, who appears to be under little pressure, could be in a tussle for a trip to Twickenham.

Rees-Zammit to return to wing for new season

Bristol sign ex-Tigers lock Wells on three-month deal

Exeter - 'Lost relatively few frontline players'

Brent Pilnick, BBC Sport, South West of England

Exeter surprised many by going from their worst-ever top flight season to beaten Prem finalists in June.

Rob Baxter's new-look coaching team has had more chance to bed in their ideas, and aside from Australia centre Len Ikitau have lost relatively few frontline players - once-capped All Black Dallas McLeod has come in to replace the Wallabies star while Exeter look strong elsewhere.

In England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, the Prem's leading points scorer Henry Slade and barnstorming number eight Greg Fisilau, Exeter possess the attacking weapons to cause any defence problems, while in Wales forward Dafydd Jenkins, Australia flanker Tom Hooper and the highly-rated Kane James they have a pack that can dominate matches.

Off the field, Exeter were taken over by Premier League football side AFC Bournemouth's owners Black Knight earlier this year – that, along with the positivity around the squad from last season, has Exeter fans dreaming of a return to the success that started just over a decade ago where they became perennial title contenders.

Injured Exeter winger Ridl to miss most of season

Exeter and Cherries share expertise after takeover

Gloucester - 'Better placed to shake off underachievers tag'

Andrew Pugh, BBC Radio Gloucestershire commentator

Gloucester have undergone considerable transition on and off the pitch and now look better placed to shake off the frequent 'serial underachievers' tag.

With Chris Boyd on board as technical director, Rob Burgess as general manager and George Skivington reverting to his preferred head coach role, the management structure looks more able to cope with the Prem's demands.

Further coaching changes have come with the arrival of Brett Deacon (forwards) and Joel Tomkins (defence).

There have been a significant number of player departures from Kingsholm, offset by the signing of the outstanding Wales international duo of Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake; with more experience added by the return of scrum-half Dan Robson and the acquisition of physical locks Joe Joyce and Jean Kleyn.

The Cherry and Whites scraped into this season's European Champions Cup, but Shedheads will probably view a top four Prem finish as the true benchmark of progress.

Harlequins - 'Fans desperate to see promised change'

Andrew Rowley, BBC Radio London commentator

Last season was possibly the most turbulent at Harlequins for almost 20 years, as a series of heavy defeats led to the club issuing a statement acknowledging that things had to change.

Chief executive Laurie Dalrymple and chairman David Morgan stated that "performances and results in the men's team are not at the level we expect at Harlequins and are not considered acceptable by anyone within the club".

A wholesale review followed and there have been big changes in the coaching staff, with former Crusaders and Australia coach Robbie Deans joining as performance director to work with head coach Jason Gilmore.

Rob Hunter, Brad Cooper, Sean Long and Jordan Turner-Hall are also involved alongside Adam Jones.

Supporters will be desperate to see that some of the promised cultural changes are reflected on the field before too long, as last season felt like a line in the sand.

Injured Dombrandt set for long spell on sidelines

Long and Turner-Hall take full-time roles at Quins

Leicester - 'Parling has brought stability'

Key signing : Aaron Wainwright, number eight

Adam Whitty, BBC Radio Leicester sports editor

Having covered Leicester Tigers for nearly a decade, I find myself in the bizarre scenario of the club having the same head coach as the previous season. That's only happened once since 2018.

Geoff Parling has finally brought some stability to English rugby's most successful club, but more than that he has set the foundations for a bright future ahead.

Leicester play in a more attacking style, led by the recently re-signed Billy Searle, and have developed a new leadership group including England trio Ollie Chessum, Freddie Steward and Jack van Poortvliet.

There hasn't been much player churn, although England lock George Martin and South African flanker Hanro Liebenberg will be big misses in the pack.

Lock Cam Henderson and the very exciting Wales flanker Aaron Wainwright will have big roles to play – and seeing Mako Vunipola in a Tigers shirt will seem strange.

After semi-final heartbreak to Northampton last year, Tigers looked like a team with a huge ceiling that needed to learn how to handle the big moments.

I expect them to be around the play-off race again, perhaps with those experiences behind them.

Listen to the Leicester Tigers Rugby Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Leicester and BBC Sounds

Vunipola planned to retire before Leicester called

Newcastle - 'Hope tempered with realism'

Dean Gray, BBC Radio Newcastle commentator

Newcastle have finished bottom of the Prem Rugby table over the past four seasons, with the Red Bull takeover last August too late to avoid that disappointment once again.

However, 23 new players have been brought into the squad this term (with around the same number exiting). The squad includes a mix of internationals including Argentina's Franco Molina, Hoskins Sotutu of New Zealand and Scotland duo Elliot Millar Mills and George Turner, seasoned campaigners like Rusi Tuima and Sam Graham, and returnees to the fold such as Josh Hodge and Chris Harris.

A revamped coaching team is in place under head coach Dan McFarland, with former Wales fly-half Stephen Jones in charge of attack and Calum MacRae returning as defence coach.

Their challenge will be to assimilate these new players into a competitive and cohesive team environment quickly.

The club's strapline is 'A New Dawn'. Ambitions and hopes are high but tempered with a realism that evolution doesn't come overnight.

Quirke excited by 'new project' at Newcastle

Northampton - 'A real belief they can win title again'

Key signing: Retaining most of squad on new contracts

Graham McKechnie, BBC Radio Northampton commentator:

For the second time in three seasons, Saints start the new campaign as defending Prem champions and they'll want to make a better defence this time around.

In 2024-25 they started as reigning champions but finished a lowly eighth in the Prem table – reaching the Champions Cup final came as some consolation, but the focus this season is all about trying to win back-to-back domestic titles.

Although they lost captain George Furbank this summer, there should be more than enough experience and leadership to make up for that, with centre Fraser Dingwall rightly taking over Furbank's role.

Henry Pollock might be grabbing all the headlines but the key players for Saints last season were the likes of Tommy Freeman, Fin Smith, Alex Mitchell and Alex Coles. This is still a young squad, but they're reaching their prime.

As always, having their key players fit at the crucial stage of the season will make all the difference, but there's real belief around Franklin's Gardens that they can win the Prem again.

Listen to The Saints Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Northampton and BBC Sounds.

Saints better prepared for Prem title defence - Dowson

Pollock signs new Northampton deal in excess of £400K

Last season was a rude awakening for Sale Sharks as their run of three straight top-four finishes was emphatically ended.

The fact that they were out of play-off contention by the January break for the Six Nations was even more damning, eventually finishing 27 points behind fourth spot, leading to the question of whether the Sharks and their physical style of play had been rumbled.

To back up some of their local talent, director of rugby Alex Sanderson has recruited a wealth of experience led by ex-Northampton and England second-rower Courtney Lawes, while there are a trio of Wales recruits in the forwards with Tomas Francis, Nicky Smith and Christ Tshuinza on board.

But the most interesting signing is that of Joe Marchant. The centre returns to the Prem after three years at Stade Francais and he has his heart set on making the England squad for next year's World Cup.

To do that, he has to play well at club level where he will fill the gap left by the influential Rob du Preez.

This feels like a pivotal season for Sanderson, who maintains the support of the club's hierarchy, to show that last season was just a blip.

The north west club will expect to compete near the top again, but the first task will be to restore order at CorpAcq Stadium after a losing record there last season.

You can hear coverage of Sale Sharks in Total Sport on BBC Radio Manchester

Saracens - 'Venter's return eagerly anticipated'

Key signing : Tomos Williams, scrum-half

Saracens are celebrating their 150th season and will set out to try to make it a campaign to remember as they aim for more consistency and a ruthless edge.

It will certainly be memorable for long-serving hooker Jamie George, who announced that it will be his last season - he has been a cornerstone of the successful era under Mark McCall that saw the club win six Premiership titles and three European Champions Cups.

The supporters will be keen to give him a send off and will also be eagerly anticipating Brendan Venter's return as director of rugby.

The South African set the platform for so much success in the past 15 years and his determination is likely to make Saracens a formidable opponent for the rest.

Number eight Tom Willis is a notable departure but the arrivals of England lock George Martin, back-rower Alfie Barbeary and Wales scrum-half Tomos Williams should add plenty, while the talented young players such as Charlie Bracken, Tobias Elliott, Angus Hall, Toby Knight and Noah Caluori should continue their progression.

Compiled by BBC Sport England's Sophie Hurcom

articles.title: Super League play-off semi-final: Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves meet in first game
articles.summary: Ahead of the their Super League play-off semi-final, Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves are aiming to assert themselves back at rugby league's top table.
articles.body:
The final curtain on the 2026 Super League season approaches.

Leeds Rhinos, Warrington Wolves, Wigan Warriors and Wakefield Trinity remain.

Off the back of a bye week courtesy of their second-placed finish, Leeds welcome Warrington on Friday for the first of two play-off semi-finals.

But with St Helens, Wigan and Hull KR taking it in turns to dominate the domestic stage over the best part of the past decade, can two of the titans of the game muscle in on the party and seal the first spot in 3 October's Super League Grand Final?

Keighran, O'Neill & Miller shortlisted for Man of Steel

Leeds Rhinos captain Handley out of play-off game

Rhinos dominate 2026 Super League Dream Team

Leeds come into the fixture following two losses against Wigan and Hull FC at home.

Looking further back, they closed out their regular campaign with three defeats in five matches.

Asked what it would take to reach the Grand Final, Leeds boss Brad Arthur said he is not worried about his side's inconsistent run of form.

"[We have to be] the best version of us. We've seen that plenty of times this year and we've played a lot of good footy," he told BBC Radio Leeds.

"Our past couple of weeks haven't been ideal but it doesn't really count for much right now. It doesn't mean anything. All those past two games showed was a couple of things that we need to tidy up which we've done during the week around execution.

"But like the first 27 rounds, all that's done is put us in a position where we're 80 minutes away from Old Trafford so that's all we got to focus on."

Leeds last reached a Grand Final in 2022, however that achievement came off the back of Richard Agar's departure in March of that season, when Leeds had won just once in their opening six games of the campaign.

In stepped Rohan Smith, who eventually strung together 11 wins from 13 matches to take them to Old Trafford where they were defeated by St Helens - however it was an even more impressive achievement given their fifth-placed finish at the end of the season.

This year, Arthur thinks his side are prepared for the rigours of a post-season campaign.

"We're ready to go. We're nice and fresh and the best version of us, we know, is good enough," he added.

"We've got to find that and we've got to do it for 80 minutes."

For Warrington, they earned their trip to Headingley having beaten reigning champions Hull KR last week in their eliminator.

Matty Ashton scored a hat-trick of tries as they ran out 35-12 winners and that win is the culmination of what has been a consistent season for the Wire.

Whereas Sam Burgess' side have tailed off in the latter stages of the campaign during his reign, this season has been different.

Ultimately they were forced to settle for third place on points difference following their final game of the regular season and they finished the campaign with nine wins from their last 11 matches.

As for the reason behind their recent success - Burgess gave an unconventional answer compared to what you might expect from a head coach.

"As coaches we just stay out of the way. We don't need to overdo anything, we leave them to it," Burgess told BBC Radio Merseyside.

"We're staying pretty humble now. Hard work will get us where we'd like to go."

Having got through one knockout game of rugby, Burgess said their preparations to face a Leeds side they have already lost to twice this season, will go ahead as normal.

"They will be aware of that, they can't hide from it," he added.

"For us it's about going there and not giving them too much space and being clinical and playing our game."

Two members of the Rhinos' squad who will not take part will be captain Ash Handley and Lachie Miller.

Man of Steel nominee Miller has been ruled out ever since he picked up a hamstring injury in Leeds' defeat by Wigan earlier this month.

Meanwhile Handley - who had been filling in at full-back for Miller - is out of Friday's game with a back injury.

Centre Jack Bird also misses out with his own hamstring injury, meaning 20-year-old Fergie McCormack will make his his fourth career start - in a huge play-off game.

Despite these omissions, Arthur believes his side have utilised their week off well.

"We had a big session on Friday try to simulate a game as close as we could and then on Monday they bounced in and nice and fresh and looked fast," he continued.

"We've made the most of it and only time will tell. We need to make sure that we cash in on the opportunity that we've been given to have the 14 days."

Meanwhile, having missed out on a play-off spot in 2025, Warrington will not let that affect their performance when they take on Leeds according to Burgess.

"It's not part of our psyche. We're really focused internally at the moment," he added.

"I don't discuss it. They don't discuss it. It's business for us on Friday night and that's something that's working for us. So we're just going to stay in that vein."

articles.title: Heat risk in sport: Are chances of death and serious illness growing with extreme temperatures?
articles.summary: BBC Sport explores the health impact of extreme heat on athletes, following the death of a Fijian rugby player in Japan in August.
articles.body:
On Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates.

After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead.

In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away".

Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer.

By noon on the day Vunilagi became ill, the temperature in Fukuoka - where Kyuden Voltex are based - had risen to 35C. The humidity was more than 75%.

In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C.

No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days.

So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change?

'Extreme heat should be treated like lightning'

There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026.

Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C.

Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages.

This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare.

Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation.

But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase.

"We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto.

"People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'.

"That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen."

Though the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme.

"Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr.

"It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away.

"We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens."

'Players need protecting from themselves'

One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health.

"I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association.

"And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes.

"It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing.

"It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training."

World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale.

But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches.

"If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day.

"Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors.

"It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment."

Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports.

On 5 June 2026, the Japan Rugby Football Union (JRFU) warned clubs heatstroke was an increasing concern during the summer, and told teams safety should be the overriding priority when planning summer training camps.

Heatstroke is a sudden, dangerous health condition which occurs when the body overheats and can no longer cool itself.

This can damage the organs, cause the intestines to release toxins and potentially be fatal within little more than an hour.

Symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion and slurring.

"Heatstroke is 100% preventable, so every single death is one too many," says Orr.

"It's not the case that athletes can handle heat better because of their fitness.

"And the bigger the body the faster it heats up, so bigger bodies are more vulnerable as well. Moving that mass around takes a lot of energy.

"So while yes, professional athletes are extraordinarily fit, that doesn't save them when the issue of concern is cooling off the body."

Amateur athletes playing for the love of the game can be at risk too.

"Whatever the elite level does, we'll see it trickle down into grassroots," says Day.

"And that's why it's crucial that the elite level of every sport sets the right example because the kids, the players of tomorrow, will absolutely copy whatever they see their heroes doing."

articles.title: WXV: Wales recall Lleucu George and Carys Cox to backline for USA
articles.summary: Wales have recalled Lleucu George and Carys Cox to their backline for Saturday's WXV Test against USA.
articles.body:
Wales have recalled Lleucu George and Carys Cox to their backline for Saturday's WXV Test against USA.

George reclaims the fly-half position with Keira Bevan reverting back to scrum-half in the absence of Seren Lockwood, who has been ruled out with a head injury.

Carys Cox replaces Seren Singleton on the wing having recovered from summer knee surgery.

They are the only two starting changes from the side which romped to a 50-19 victory over South Africa last Friday, while there are three new faces on the bench in Molly Reardon, Sian Jones and Nikita Prothero.

Alex Callender and Kate Williams will once again co-captain the side at Cardiff Arms Park, while Georgia Evans will win her 50th cap.

Wales deliver performance of serious promise

USA stun Ireland with comeback WXV win in Dublin

"It's great to see Keira Bevan back at nine, I thought she did extremely well at 10, but Lleucu George has got a new lease of life in training and fingers crossed, everything will just keep going," said Wales head coach Sean Lynn.

"Carys Cox will bring that athleticism, she will always look to beat the first defender, she always wants the ball in hand and her work rate off the ball is outstanding."

Speaking about Evans reaching her half century, Lynn added: "I take my hat off to Georgia.

"Some of the heat she took during the World Cup and she still goes out there, brave with that bow in her hair, I just think she's an absolute inspiration to young girls."

Lynn will be looking to make it three wins in a row on Saturday having also beaten the Barbarians in June.

But they face a USA side ranked sixth in the world and bouyed by their impressive comeback victory against Ireland last weekend.

"We know it's going to be a really tough competition, to beat Ireland in Ireland takes a good side," Lynn said.

"They've got a very good set piece, you can see that Jonathan Humphreys [former Wales and Ospreys coach] has gone in there and tightened up their pack.

"They've got individuals like Hope Rogers and their number eight Georgie Perris-Redding will captain with passion. In my eyes there's a very exciting battle there against Alex Callender."

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Replacements: Reardon, Pyrs, E Jones, Crabb, Aiono, S Jones, De Vera, Prothero

articles.title: Prem Rugby: the investor rush into English top-flight rugby union
articles.summary: Prem Rugby seemed on the brink of disaster after Worcester, Wasps and London Irish went bust, but there is renewed confidence and fresh money in the league.
articles.body:
Simon Massie-Taylor pulled up outside Newcastle's Kingston Park stadium, and saw fear.

The unannounced arrival of Prem Rugby's chief executive at one of the league's clubs had rarely been a good sign.

Massie-Taylor started the role in January 2022. In the 18 months that followed, Wasps, Worcester and London Irish, with finances stretched out of shape by Covid, had flamed out of the English top flight.

"When those clubs were going into administration, the common denominator was their leadership leaving the room," remembers Massie-Taylor.

"The owners, the chief executives, everyone went.

"So it was basically up to me, [Rugby Players Association general secretary] Christian Day and [Rugby Football Union director of legal and governance] Angus Bujalski to go in and say, 'we're terribly sorry, this is what's happened, this is what it means for you'.

"Telling anyone that they've lost their job is one of the worst bits of having a job. But when it comes to sport, for the people that work in those clubs, it's not just a job, it's a way of life. It was horrible."

So when Massie-Taylor pitched up at Newcastle last year, with the club limping from payroll to payroll, onlookers feared the worse.

"Some of the players and staff, when they first saw me, thought I was this grim reaper figure coming to deliver another bad news story," he said.

Instead he ushered Newcastle's staff into a room decked out in the blue and silver branding of Red Bull.

Backed by a hype video filled with signature extreme sport stunts, executives from the energy drink giant, fresh off a flight, spelled out a grand vision for the Prem's bottom club.

"There were people in that room in tears, it was pretty special," said Massie-Taylor.

That investment was a pivot point for the league.

Massie-Taylor remembers how low the bar was to buy into the Prem in his first few, stressful years. "It was 'do you exist, have you got a criminal record, do you actually have any money?," he says.

But Red Bull's arrival, sealed and delivered in August 2025, marked a sea change.

Since then Black Knight - the owners of Premier League side Bournemouth - have bought up Exeter Chiefs, billionaire industrialist Sir James Dyson has taken a 50% share of Bath and financier Steve Zander has made a multi-million pound investment into Northampton Saints. , external

More outside investment is expected soon, with Gloucester and Leicester among those in conversations.

"Investor interest in the league has increased significantly in the last 12 months, certainly the last six," says Massie-Taylor, who convened a summit for prospective buyers in London in June and is heading to the United States in October to press flesh and make the case.

His confidence is shared by more impartial experts.

Matthew Wheeler helped broker Red Bull's takeover of Newcastle, but his specialist investment group A&W Capital has made deals across a variety of sports and media.

"I don't think you're drunk from the Kool-Aid to have belief in the Prem, there definitely is a momentum behind it," he says.

Andrew Umbers is a co-founder of Oakwell Sports Advisory, which had a similar role in Exeter's takeover.

"We put Exeter in front just over 110 sports investors and we had interest probably from around 30," he says. "That interest came from North America, Asia and continental Europe."

It is quite the difference from when Massie-Taylor would entertain enquiries from anyone with proof of identity, a clean chargesheet and a positive bank balance.

There are a few factors that are happy coincidence, rather than canny design.

The value of sports teams generally has risen steeply. The sale of the LA Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.3bn) this summer is the prime example.

Wheeler puts the spike down to the guaranteed eyeballs sport attracts in a fragmented media world, its relative resistance to disruption by artificial intelligence as a product and the prestige and scarcity value of owning a sports team.

Prem Rugby was also on an upward growth trajectory before the Covid pandemic hit. Even with the loss of three teams, a return to normality has allowed the league to rediscover that groove.

A brand of the heft of Red Bull getting involved in the league, undoubtedly sparked interest elsewhere.

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

However, proactive changes have played a part.

An independent financial monitoring panel has kept across all Prem club finances for the past couple of seasons, and is designed to prevent dangerous levels of risk and spending. That has reassured investors.

With a funding deal with the Rugby Football Union and broadcast partnership with TNT Sports locked in for several seasons, there is stability for the foreseeable.

A calendar shift , external has meant England internationals are available more often to their clubs, raising the wattage on the domestic game's star power.

And, while Massie-Taylor won't say it himself, he has inspired confidence. A former investment banker, he understands what prospective buyers are looking for.

"The governance is important because the first thing an investor wants to know is can they rely on the management and is the league going to be well run.

"You may be buying into an individual team, but you're really buying into the league.

"You can have the most successful team you want, but if the league's not successful, it doesn't mean anything."

Massie-Taylor's most important decision might be his most controversial.

He backed the ring-fencing of the league, scrapping relegation and bringing new teams in via a tender process rather than achievements on the pitch.

This season is the first to be played out without even a hint of jeopardy at the bottom of the table.

While some see a betrayal of sporting tradition, the change gives Prem Rugby a point of difference over lower-level football sides competing for the same investment.

No possible drop down the leagues, no danger of a distressed asset.

"It is a real thing for US investors," says Massie-Taylor.

"There was a fear and, to some extent, a handbrake on investment because of that financial jeopardy."

It is just one aspect of the league that makes prospective American buyers comfortable.

The upper and, from this season, lower limits on how much Prem clubs can spend on players' salaries are common in Stateside sport, as is the equitable sharing of media revenues.

There has also been a shift to centralise deals and maximise revenues.

A proposal to have one kit manufacturer for the whole league - something seen in America's 'big four' leagues (NBA, NFL, MLB and NHL) - has been floated in the past.

"For an investor, owning a Prem Rugby team is more is more like owning an NFL team than it is like owning a Premier League football team [in that regard]," says Wheeler.

It was noticeable that Brett Gosper, formerly the head of World Rugby, now leading NFL Europe, was on hand at Prem Rugby's investor summit to underline those parallels.

The combination of features of a franchise league, with the long rivalries and established, loyal fanbases that a start-up competition lacks, makes the Prem a rare prospect.

"American investors are interested in under-commercialised sport, below the tier-one leagues such as Premier League, NFL or the IPL, that are at a turning point in their cycle," says Umbers.

"Rugby is not a big sport in America, so there has got to be some education going on," he says.

"But will American investors be interested once they understand the dynamics? Yes."

Massie-Taylor knows the margins are narrow.

A 10-team league cannot afford any more clubs to go under. There are financial debts and a dependency on owner generosity across the league.

"We've proved there's opportunity going forward," he says.

"The thing that's niggling us now is the fear that we don't make the most of it. That's the pressure we all feel to really crack on."

It isn't just the players aiming to start the season fast.

articles.title: England v New Zealand: Maddie Feaunati returns to back row for hosts
articles.summary: Maddie Feaunati returns to bring big-game experience and dynamism to the back row as England take on a resurgent New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.
articles.body:
Maddie Feaunati returns to bring big-game experience and dynamism to the back row as England take on a resurgent New Zealand, their closest challengers at the top of the world rankings, in front of more than 50,000 fans at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.

Feaunati comes in at number eight, with Alex Matthews shifting to blind-side flanker and Abi Burton to the bench.

The three starters all featured in England's Women's Rugby World Cup final win against Canada, one year ago on Sunday.

England, whose 39-match winning streak was halted by a 26-26 draw against Canada last weekend, make their other changes in the front row.

Props Mackenzie Carson and Sarah Bern come in to start with Hannah Botterman and Maud Muir poised to add power off the bench.

Bryony Field, whose involvement in the international set-up before this autumn was limited to age-grade appearances half a decade ago, retains her place at starting hooker ahead of May Campbell.

Amy Cokayne and Connie Powell are both missing through injury, while Lark Atkin Davies has only recently given birth.

England's backline remains unchanged with Helena Rowland at inside centre and Jess Breach, Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Ellie Kildunne making up the back three.

Natasha Hunt, Tatyana Heard and Emma Sing are the specialist backs on the bench.

Live on BBC iPlayer and BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary

"We're moving forward in the right direction whilst building depth in our cover," said head coach John Mitchell.

"New Zealand are playing good rugby at the moment and it's no surprise to see them raise their standards.

"Test matches against the best teams in the world are what we relish and look forward to, especially at Allianz Stadium."

New Zealand were the last team to beat the Red Roses, upsetting the tournament favourites in the final of the previous Women's Rugby World Cup in November 2022.

England have won the teams' three meetings since - most recently running out 49-31 winners in October 2024 - but the Black Ferns have won all seven Tests they have played this year under new coach Whitney Hansen.

"Our players are built different, we're made for these moments," said Hansen, who is the daughter of former All Blacks coach Steve Hansen.

"We've continued to grow each week and we're excited to put our rugby identity to the test against England, who are currently number one in the world. "

Among Hansen's selection is wing Ayesha Leti-I'iga, who scored two tries in her team's World Cup final win over England, and teenage full-back Braxton Sorensen-McGee, who was one of the stars of the 2025 tournament.

articles.title: Darcy Graham: Injury rules winger out of Scotland's autumn Tests
articles.summary: Scotland's record try-scorer Darcy Graham is to miss the autumn internationals against New Zealand, Australia and Japan with a ruptured bicep.
articles.body:
Scotland's record try-scorer Darcy Graham is to miss the autumn internationals with a bicep injury.

The 29-year-old Edinburgh winger has 38 tries from his 57 caps but will not have the chance to add to that tally in home Tests against New Zealand, Australia and Japan.

Edinburgh head coach Sean Everitt revealed Graham is facing at least 12 weeks on the sidelines as he recovers from a rupture.

Describing the collision incident as "pretty freakish", Everitt, said: "That's not good news for us and not good news for him, especially with the autumn series coming up."

Scotland continue their Nations Championship fixtures against New Zealand at Murrayfield on 7 November, with Australia and Japan in Edinburgh on the following weekends.

The inaugural series will culminate with a finals weekend at Twickenham on 27 and 28 November.

In the summer, Scotland beat Argentina and Fiji either side of a 42-28 defeat in South Africa, which has Gregor Townsend's side sitting second behind France in the northern hemisphere standings.

articles.title: Scotland: Rachel McLachlan and Evie Wills back from injury to face Australia
articles.summary: Rachel McLachlan and Evie Wills return from injury to start for Scotland against Australia in their final home match of the WXV Series on Saturday.
articles.body:
Rachel McLachlan and Evie Wills return from injury to start for Scotland against Australia in their final home match of the WXV Series on Saturday.

Sarah Bonar and Hannah Ramsay also come into the starting line-up as interim head coach Dave Butcher makes four changes following the 66-14 defeat by New Zealand.

Butcher believes facing Canada and New Zealand has helped the development of his team despite suffering two heavy defeats.

"Coming out of two really, really hard games, the feeling is that we got stress tested a lot in those games, which has allowed us to accelerate what we need to do a little bit more, rather than playing a game where we're not too sure whether that will work against the world's best," he said.

"If you look at progression from game one to game two, and the pieces that we wanted to get after, we definitely saw some improvements, especially, I thought, in the contact area from game one to game two."

Phillips misses Australia visit as Wassell ruled out of series

Bartlett urges Scots to make history against Australia

Feaunati returns as England brace for Black Ferns

Montpellier's McLachlan comes into the line-up at openside flanker, with Sale Sharks' Eva Donaldson dropping to the bench for the match at Hive Stadium, Edinburgh, being shown live on BBC Alba and BBC iPlayer (kick-off 16:10 BST).

Glasgow Warriors' Wills starts at outside centre in place of Edinburgh's Rachel Philipps, who misses out through injury.

Edinburgh's Ramsay, who was a replacement against Canada and the Black Ferns, makes her second Scotland start at full-back, with clubmate Chloe Rollie dropping to the bench.

Harlequins lock Bonar, who came off the bench last time out, makes her first appearance in a Scotland starting XV since the 2025 Rugby World Cup quarter-final against England and replaces Trailfinders' injured Emma Wassell.

Bristol Bears hooker Lana Skeldon will become the second-most capped Scotland women's player when making her 90th appearance.

Having made her first start against the Black Ferns, Glasgow's Ceitidh Ainsworth keeps her place at scrum-half.

Edinburgh scrum-half Leia Brebner-Holden is named in the matchday squad for the first time this campaign after overcoming injury.

articles.title: Red Roses vs New Zealand: Mackenzie Carson, Sarah Bern and Maddie Feaunati all included in side for match at Allianz Stadium
articles.summary: Head coach John Mitchell has made three changes to the Red Roses starting XV for Saturday’s match against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium in the WXV Global Series; England's incredible winning run came to an end in nail-biting draw with Canada last week
articles.body:
Props Bern and Carson start in the front row alongside hooker Field who earns her second start, while Maddie Feaunati is recalled at No 8 meaning a switch to blindside flanker for vice-captain Alex Matthews.

Morwenna Talling and Lilli Ives Campion continue in the second row, and back row Sadia Kabeya completes the pack.

Head coach John Mitchell said: "We're moving forward in the right direction while building depth in our cover. Now we look forward to renewing a rivalry with a New Zealand side we haven't played since 2024. They are playing good rugby at the moment and it's no surprise to see them raise their standards.

"Test matches against the best teams in the world are what we relish and look forward to, especially at Allianz Stadium."

The backline remains unchanged from the team that began last weekend's draw against Canada. Lucy Packer and Zoe Harrison are the half-backs with Helena Rowland and captain Megan Jones forming the centre partnership.

Claudia Moloney-MacDonald retains her spot on the wing following two tries down at Sandy Park. Ellie Kildunne and Jess Breach are also named in the back three.

Among the replacements, Natasha Hunt and Tatyana Heard are back in the 23 and Emma Sing is set for her first WXV Global Series appearance.

Over 50,000 supporters will be in attendance at Allianz Stadium on Saturday for the 34th encounter between the Red Roses and the Black Ferns.

The Red Roses are unbeaten across their last 53 matches on home soil since a 20-25 defeat to New Zealand at the Twickenham Stoop in November 2016.

They have won each of their last 13 at the Allianz Stadium but New Zealand have lost just one of their 17 games since the start of 2025.
